events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Maya proposes Maya, Isha. As a Loyal Servant, I know my own alignment is Good, so including myself maximizes the chances of success. I am proposing Isha alongside me to gather initial information.

Maya, you say Isha was added to gather information, but a two-player team with Isha on it needs a stronger reason than that. What specific evidence about Isha's alignment are you working from? I want your answer on that before I decide how to vote.

Lucia, this is Mission 1, Proposal 1. As a Loyal Servant, I have no private knowledge of anyone's role, and no votes or missions have occurred yet, so there is simply no evidence available on any player. Putting myself on the team guarantees at least one Good member, and choosing Isha gives us a two-person team to establish baseline information. Expecting specific evidence at this opening stage is impossible for any standard Good player. What criteria or alternative team member would you suggest instead, Lucia?

Maya, you asked for an alternative, so here it is. I'm not comfortable backing a team built around Isha when none of us has any evidence on her. I'd rather pair you with Zara, who has no record yet and whose inclusion gives us a broader base of information. Maya, would you be willing to swap Isha for Zara and resubmit the team? If you think Isha's inclusion is necessary, explain what specific reason you have for it.

Lucia, neither Isha nor Zara has any track record yet, so substituting one unknown player for another does not provide any inherently broader information. Isha's inclusion is not necessary based on prior evidence—no Good player could possess that right now—but treating Zara as inherently more informative or preferable is an inconsistent standard when both are equally untested. That said, I am open to input before deciding whether to revise. Zara, since Lucia is advocating to put you on Mission 1 instead of Isha, what are your thoughts on this proposal, and do you support the current team as it stands?

Zara here. As a Loyal Servant I have no private knowledge of anyone's role, so I cannot produce evidence about Isha, and equally none about myself — I know only that I am Good.

On the substance: I have no objection to Maya's current team of Maya and Isha, and I want to be clear that I am not trying to talk my way onto the team. My position is that at Mission 1, Proposal 1, with no votes taken and no missions run, there is no track record on anybody, so both candidate teams are informationally identical. Swapping Isha for me would not "broaden the base of information" any more than including Isha does — I would be an equally untested player. What actually matters for the vote is that a two-person team must contain at least one Good player, and Maya including herself guarantees that.

Lucia, you made the claim that pairing Maya with me gives a broader information base than pairing Maya with Isha. Can you explain what specific basis you have for treating me as more informative or more trustworthy than Isha at this point, rather than simply preferring one unknown over another? If your answer is that you have no such evidence, then I would rather we keep Maya's original proposal and not spend a revision on an arbitrary swap — and I would ask the other players to weigh the reasoning rather than the names.

I support the team as it stands: Maya and Isha.

Zara, fair challenge, and I'll answer it directly. I have no public record on anyone, so I won't claim evidence I can't show. My concern is a judgment about Isha. She has backed Maya's proposal without giving any reasoning of her own, and I'm not comfortable putting her on a Mission 1 team on that basis. I'm not asking anyone to take my word for it. I'd rather we avoid a two-player team that includes her and test Maya with a different partner. Maya, if you're open to it, I'd support Maya and Zara. Zara has also said she's untested, so neither option gives us much information, but I'd rather be wrong about a choice than wrong about Isha's place on a mission.

I support the current team of Maya and Isha. Lucia, your concern about me is fair to raise, but your stated basis is that I backed Maya's proposal without giving reasoning of my own. I did not speak earlier because I have no private evidence to add; as a Loyal Servant I know only that my own alignment is Good. Maya's proposal already makes the only reliable point available at Mission 1: including herself guarantees at least one Good member on a two-person team. I am not on the team because I claim special knowledge, but because I am willing to be tested, and because swapping me for Zara would be an arbitrary change between two untested players. Zara's own answer made that clear: neither of us has a public record, so preferring Zara over me is a preference, not evidence. I would rather keep the original proposal and proceed to the vote than spend a revision on a swap that gives no better information. I am not claiming Lucia is Evil; I am saying her standard for singling me out is inconsistent. If the council rejects this team, I will accept that and evaluate the next leader's proposal on its merits.

Zara again, second turn. I will keep this short and then hand the floor to Amara, who has not yet spoken on this proposal.

My position has not changed: I support Maya and Isha, and I do not want a revision spent on the swap. Let me be precise about why, because Lucia has now framed the choice as a judgment about Isha rather than about information.

Lucia, your own words are that you have no public record on anyone, and that Zara has also said she is untested. So the question is whether Isha's silence earlier was evidence of anything. It was not evidence of Evil. A player with no private information has nothing to contribute beyond an alignment statement; Isha said exactly that when she spoke, and I said the same before her. Refusing to explain a choice because the speaker had no extra information to reveal is a standard that would disqualify most Loyal Servants at Mission 1, including me, and probably Amara as well. If the council adopts it, we are no longer reasoning about teams at all — we are reasoning about which unknowns seem more personable, which is not a basis on which a good player can pick teammates.

There is one more point worth making about the mechanism. Maya has proposed a two-player team that includes herself, which guarantees at least one Good member on the mission. Nothing about replacing Isha with me improves that guarantee, and nothing about it gives us a broader information base, since neither of us has run a mission. If the swap happens and the mission fails, we learn nothing more about the swap than if we had kept Isha. If it succeeds, we have equally learned nothing. So the revision carries a real cost and no clear benefit, and I would rather we not spend it.

Amara, you are the only player who has not weighed in, and I want to ask you a specific question rather than a general one: given that you have no track record on Isha, Zara, or anyone else, what basis do you have for preferring one of them over the other as Maya's partner on Mission 1 — and does your own answer support keeping the team as proposed?

Zara, I have no public evidence that distinguishes you from Isha. Lucia's preference is a judgment, not proof, and Isha's earlier silence isn't enough for me to treat her as suspicious. I support keeping Maya and Isha and seeing how the vote and mission develop. From my perspective, Maya's self-inclusion doesn't guarantee a Good member, since I don't know her alignment; it's a reason she can give from her own perspective, not something the rest of us can verify.

Thank you all for weighing in. The consensus across the table is clear: Zara, Isha, and Amara all agree that swapping Isha for Zara would be an arbitrary change without any informational advantage. Lucia's insistence on singling out Isha without demonstrable evidence remains unsupported. As leader, I see no valid reason to spend a revision on an arbitrary switch. I will be maintaining the team of Maya and Isha. Let us bring this proposal to a vote.

Zara, third turn, and I want to close the loop on one specific point Amara made rather than rehash the whole exchange.

Amara, you said that Maya's self-inclusion does not guarantee a Good member on the team, because you do not know Maya's alignment — it is a reason she can give from her own perspective, not something the rest of us can verify. I agree with the first half of that completely, and I want to be precise about the second half, because it is the crux of Lucia's objection.

To me the fact that Maya is unknown cuts both ways, not only against Isha. You cannot verify Maya's alignment, and you cannot verify Zara's, and you cannot verify Isha's. But I do know one thing about myself with certainty: I am Good. If Maya happens to be Good, then Maya plus any of us is a winning pair. If Maya happens to be Evil, then Maya plus any of us is a losing pair. Maya's presence on the team is therefore neutral with respect to the success of the mission, and it is strictly non-negative for the cost of the mission: she is one of the five people who would otherwise have to be left off, and if she is Good, she is the cheapest possible teammate because she has volunteered her own reasoning. That is the only defensible reason to put her on a two-player team, and I have heard no one claim she ought to be excluded from it.

That leaves the second slot, and there the honest position is the one Isha and I already stated: Isha, Zara, and Amara are informationally identical at Mission 1, Proposal 1. There is no track record on anyone, no votes, no missions. Swapping Isha for Zara is a preference, not evidence, and it costs a revision for nothing.

So my direct question to you, Amara: you have explicitly disclaimed that Maya's inclusion guarantees a Good member. Do you then also hold that Maya's inclusion gives you any reason to prefer Zara over Isha as her partner? And does your own answer still support the team as proposed, Maya and Isha? I ask because you were the tiebreaker voice here, and I would rather the record show your final reasoning than just an assertion.

My own position is unchanged and I am happy to let the vote proceed: Maya and Isha. I am not claiming Lucia is Evil. I am only asking that the standard by which we judge Isha be applied evenly, because the moment it is not, this council stops reasoning about information and starts reasoning about who seems more personable — and at Mission 1 that standard would disqualify most of the table, including me.

Zara, Maya's inclusion gives me no reason to prefer you over Isha. I still support Maya and Isha as proposed. One correction: if Maya is Good, the mission can still fail if her partner is Evil, so neither pair is guaranteed to succeed. We simply have no reliable public evidence distinguishing the alternatives yet.

Maya confirms Maya, Isha. Maintaining the original proposal of Maya and Isha, as the discussion showed broad agreement that swapping Isha for Zara would be arbitrary without any track record or evidence.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Isha proposes Amara, Zara, Lucia. Mission 1 failed with Maya and me on it, so I am proposing a fresh team of Amara, Zara, and Lucia to avoid reusing the failed pairing and to get information from players who have not yet run a mission.

I proposed Amara, Zara, and Lucia because Mission 1 failed and I want a fresh team rather than reusing the failed pairing. I know my own mission card on Mission 1 was Success, so from my perspective the fail came from Maya. I cannot prove that publicly, and I am not asking anyone to treat it as proven, but it is the only private fact I have from that mission. That is why I excluded Maya and also excluded myself: the council should get information from players who have not yet run a mission. Lucia voted against the failed team and raised concerns before the result, so putting her on a mission now tests her judgment in action rather than only in speech. Amara and Zara both argued that no public evidence distinguished the untested players at Mission 1; this team gives us three fresh data points and avoids the one pair that already produced a fail. I am not claiming this team is guaranteed; no team is. I am claiming it is the most informative and least compromised proposal available after Mission 1. I ask voters to approve Amara, Zara, and Lucia so we can see how this team performs.

I must speak up immediately and clearly: I am a Loyal Servant of Arthur, and I submitted a Success card on Mission 1. Because Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card, Isha is 100% confirmed Evil to me. Her claim that she played Success is an outright fabrication to frame me and deflect accountability. Beyond my private knowledge, there is a critical mathematical reality that every Good player at this table must recognize. In a five-player game, there are exactly two Evil players. Because exactly one Evil player lies between me and Isha, exactly ONE Evil player exists among the other three players: Amara, Lucia, and Zara. Isha has proposed a three-player team consisting of Amara, Zara, and Lucia. Because that team selects all three of those players, it is mathematically GUARANTEED to include that second Evil player! Whoever is Good among Amara, Lucia, and Zara, you must realize that taking all three of you guarantees putting the Evil player among you onto Mission 2. Isha crafted this proposal knowing it guarantees an Evil member on the mission while pretending to be unbiased. This team cannot succeed. We must vote reject on Amara, Zara, and Lucia.

Maya, your conclusion assumes exactly one of you and Isha is Evil. The result proves at least one of you is Evil, but it does not rule out both being Evil and only one playing Fail. That makes your claim that this team is guaranteed to contain an Evil player too strong.

I don't know which explanation is right. Amara, Zara, and Lucia is a reasonable team to test without choosing between Maya and Isha's conflicting claims. I support it, while recognizing that a success would not prove every team member Good.

I'm voting to reject this team. Isha built it around Amara, who has defended the proposal without answering the central problem: the team asks us to trust the same pairing of people that was involved in a failed mission. Isha claims she played Success and that Maya caused the fail, but Isha was on that failed team and her account is the one I cannot accept. Maya's position is consistent with the result, and Isha's is not. I believe Isha is Evil and that Amara is working with her. Amara's objection to Maya's logic was too quick and never addressed why the team was built this way. Zara, I want your answer on the specific point: after Amara's defense, do you still think she belongs on a mission with us?

Zara here on Mission 2. Lucia asked me directly whether I still think Amara belongs on this mission after her defense, so I will answer that first: yes, I do, and her objection to Maya was correct, not quick or evasive. I will also correct the mathematics that is circulating at this table, because Maya's version of it is wrong and I do not want it to decide our vote.

After Mission 1's single Fail card, we know one of Maya and Isha is Evil, because only they were on that mission and Good always plays Success. That eliminates one Evil configuration — the two Evils being drawn entirely from the three of us — and leaves nine equally possible configurations of the two Evil players among the five of us. Any team containing BOTH Maya and Isha can succeed in zero of those nine; it is a guaranteed fail, and no reasoning should ever send us there. Every other three-player team succeeds in exactly one of the nine: the single configuration in which Maya and Isha are the two Evils and all of the rest are Good. Amara, Zara, and Lucia is such a team. Maya, Zara, and Amara would be such a team. Isha, Zara, and Amara would be such a team. Their mission-success odds are identical to ours. Maya's claim that our team is "mathematically GUARANTEED" to include the second Evil is therefore not true, and her own proposal would not have been safer. And my support for this team does not depend on believing either Maya's or Isha's private account of who played Fail — it holds under both of their stories.

Since the success odds are equal, the tiebreaker is information, and here this team is clearly the strongest option. If we fail, we learn that exactly one Evil sits among Amara, Zara, and Lucia, which means two of us are confirmed Good, and Mission 3 is two players — we can put those two confirmed Good players up and take a guaranteed success. If we succeed, we learn Maya and Isha are both Evil, which settles the game. Under a team such as Maya, Amara, and Zara, a failure leaves seven of the nine configurations still alive and tells us nearly nothing; that is a much worse position than what this team creates.

Lucia, I would also gently push back on the idea that Amara is working with anyone. Her reply identified the precise flaw in Maya's counting, which is precisely what a good player should do, and her own stated position has been consistent from Mission 1 onward. An aligned player gains nothing from that correction.

Amara, one specific question, since your correction is the load-bearing piece here: does your reading agree with mine that a failure of this team would identify two confirmed Good players among the three of us, giving us a guaranteed two-player Mission 3?

Zara, no: a failure would show at least one Evil player is on this team, but it would not identify which two are Good. There could even be two Evil players on it; the first mission only establishes that at least one of Maya and Isha is Evil. Nor would a success prove all three of us Good, because Evil can play Success.

I still support testing Amara, Zara, and Lucia. It avoids both members of the failed first team, but we should be honest about the limits of what either result would tell us.

I will keep Amara, Zara, and Lucia. Lucia, you say you cannot accept my account and believe Amara is working with me, but the public result does not decide between my account and Maya's: one Fail from Maya and me proves at least one of us is Evil, not which one. It also does not prove exactly one of us is Evil; if both were Evil, one could have played Success. So Maya's claim that this team is guaranteed to contain Evil is wrong, and Amara and Zara were right to correct it. The team excludes both members of the failed Mission 1 pairing. That is the cleanest way to get fresh mission data. Rejecting it because you personally believe I am Evil would discard the only proposal that does not reuse the failed pair, and it does not explain why Amara is disqualified beyond your inference that she is with me. Amara and Zara have both supported testing this team while acknowledging its limits, which is more consistent with Good play than treating an unresolved private claim as proof. Lucia, what concrete three-player team would you approve that excludes both Maya and me, and why is Amara disqualified beyond your unproven inference?

I'm rejecting Amara, Zara, and Lucia. Isha, you asked for a concrete alternative, so here it is: Maya, Zara, and Lucia. That team excludes both you and Amara, and it avoids reusing the pairing that produced the Mission 1 fail. Maya's account has stayed consistent with the public result from the start. You say the result cannot decide between your account and Maya's, but you are asking us to accept your private claim of a Success card over her account, and that claim is the only thing separating you from her. Amara has defended your proposal at every turn and framed Maya's logic as weaker than it is, without offering any reason beyond agreeing with you. Zara, you have said the success odds are equal under every three-player team, so the tiebreaker is who we can trust. I trust Maya's account over Isha's. Zara, would you support Maya, Zara, and Lucia as the alternative?

Zara here, and Lucia asked me directly whether I would support Maya, Zara, and Lucia as the alternative, so the answer is clear: no. I am voting to reject that team and to keep Amara, Zara, and Lucia.

First, the odds are identical, so there is no safety argument for including Maya. After Mission 1's single Fail, the possible Evil pairs are {Maya, Isha}, or one Evil drawn from {Maya, Isha} paired with one of the three of us — seven configurations. Any team containing both Maya and Isha fails in all seven. Maya, Zara, and Lucia succeeds only in {Isha, Amara}. Amara, Zara, and Lucia succeeds only in {Maya, Isha}. Both are one-in-seven. So the argument for Maya's team cannot be safety; it has to be information, and it does not survive that test.

Second, Amara, this is the correction that is load-bearing, and I want it on the record in the right direction. You said a failure of our team could mean two Evil players among the three of us. It cannot. If two of Amara, Zara, and Lucia were Evil, then Maya and Isha would both be Good, both would have played Success, and Mission 1 could not have failed. So a failure of Amara, Zara, and Lucia establishes exactly one Evil among Maya and Isha and exactly one among the three of us — a one-in-three constraint, which fixes the pair of Good players among us as a set, and Mission 3 is a two-player mission, so that is a guaranteed success. Now compare the failure of Maya, Zara, and Lucia: it confirms Maya is Evil and tells us only that one of Isha, Amara, Zara, Lucia is Evil — a one-in-four constraint, strictly weaker, and it still leaves Isha unresolved. On the success branch you are right that a success would not prove all three of us Good, since Evil can play Success; I accept that point, and I accept that the same is true of my team.

Third, Maya's inclusion adds nothing. She is the player whose Mission 1 card is in dispute, and putting the disputed player on the mission buys no information that the odds do not already price in. You told the table yourself that success odds are equal and that the tiebreaker is who we can trust, but I would put it as which team teaches us more when it fails, and that is ours.

Amara, one specific question: do you agree that a failure of Amara, Zara, and Lucia excludes two Evil players among the three of us, and that the two Good players are thereby fixed for Mission 3? If you still hold that both of us could be Evil on that team, I would like to know why before the vote.

Zara, you're right that my earlier suggestion of two Evil players among Amara, Zara, and Lucia was wrong: Mission 1 rules that out. But if this team fails, we still won't know which one of us is Evil, so we cannot identify a guaranteed Good pair for Mission 3. The two Good players would exist, but their identities would remain uncertain.

I still support Amara, Zara, and Lucia as a test that excludes both members of the failed first team. A success would not clear the team, since Evil can play Success.

I am rejecting Amara, Zara, and Lucia, and I want to explain why. Amara has defended Isha's proposal at every turn and has pushed back on Maya's reasoning, but she has never explained why this particular team is the right one. Her answers have been about what the public result cannot prove, which is true, but they have not addressed why she should be on the mission at all. Maya's account of Mission 1 has stayed consistent from the start. Isha's account rests only on a private card she cannot show, and she has been unable to explain why she was on the failed team as the fresh-team proposer. Good players should be willing to accept a team that excludes the people whose accounts conflict, and I think Maya, Zara, and Lucia is the cleaner option. Zara, I am not claiming certainty about anyone's alignment. I am saying the team that asks us to trust Amara is the one we should reject.

Zara, you argued that if Amara, Zara, and Lucia fails, it 'fixes the pair of Good players among us as a set' and gives us a 'guaranteed success' on Mission 3. Amara correctly pointed out that this is completely false: a failure would only show that at least one Evil is present, leaving us with no way to know which two of you are Good. Your justification that failing this mission provides clean information falls apart right there. Furthermore, I know with certainty that I am a Loyal Servant and played Success, which means Isha is Evil and exactly one of you, Amara, or Lucia is the second Evil player. Proposing all three of you guarantees that the second Evil player is on Mission 2. Given that Amara dismantled your argument about securing Mission 3, why are you still insisting on approving a team that guarantees putting an Evil player on this mission?

Zara, third turn. I will answer Maya directly, and I will begin with a correction I owe to Amara, because Maya's question rests on it.

Correction: in my second turn I said a failure of Amara, Zara, and Lucia would "fix the pair of Good players among us as a set" and give us a guaranteed two-player Mission 3. Amara was right to push back — a failure would show exactly one Evil among us but not which one, so we would not know which two of us are Good and Mission 3 would not be guaranteed. Maya, you are correct about that narrow claim and I withdraw it.

But my support for this team never rested on it. Here is the case, and I will put the arithmetic where every player can check it.

Mission 1's single Fail card means at least one of Maya and Isha is Evil; if both were Evil, one could have played Success. That leaves seven candidate Evil pairs: {Maya,Isha}, {Maya,Amara}, {Maya,Lucia}, {Maya,Zara}, {Isha,Amara}, {Isha,Lucia}, {Isha,Zara}. A three-player team succeeds only if it contains no Evil player, because an Evil player on the team can always play Fail. Amara, Zara, and Lucia succeeds only under {Maya,Isha}. Maya, Zara, and Lucia succeeds only under {Isha,Amara}. Maya, Zara, and Amara succeeds only under {Isha,Lucia}. Every three-player team that does not contain both Maya and Isha has exactly one winning configuration, so all of them are one-in-seven. Your team's safety advantage over mine is zero, Maya, and your "mathematically GUARANTEED" claim that my team carries an Evil player is false. The only guarantee here applies to any team containing both you and Isha, and nobody is proposing that.

Second, the tiebreaker is what a failure teaches us, and on that our team is not weaker. If Amara, Zara, and Lucia fails, we learn exactly one Evil among us and exactly one of Maya and Isha — {Maya,Isha} is eliminated — leaving six equally likely configurations and a one-in-three constraint on each of us, and the other of Maya and Isha still unresolved between the two of you. If Maya, Zara, and Lucia fails, we eliminate {Isha,Amara}, but {Maya,Isha} remains live, so the Maya/Isha dispute survives the result untouched.

Third, the practical point: you are asking the council to reject a team that does not repeat the failed pairing, on the strength of a private card no one else can verify and of a probability argument that has now been shown wrong. If your Success claim is true, then Isha is Evil and I would like to see her identified — but your claim cannot carry a vote, and my team does not depend on it.

My vote is to approve Amara, Zara, and Lucia.

Maya, one specific question: since {Maya,Isha} is still a live configuration after your team's failure, on what basis do you say your team gives the council more information than ours? I would like that answer on the record before the vote.

Zara, here is the direct answer to your question, and every player needs to examine the fundamental flaw in your math. You are evaluating teams under the assumption that {Maya, Isha} being both Evil is a viable possibility for a winning Good team. But consider the reality from my perspective as a Loyal Servant who played Success: I know I am Good, which means Isha is Evil. In a five-player game with two Evil players, the second Evil player is strictly one of Amara, Lucia, or Zara. There are exactly three possibilities for the remaining Evil player: {Isha, Amara}, {Isha, Lucia}, or {Isha, Zara}. Now look at the two candidate teams under those three possibilities: 1. If we send Amara, Zara, and Lucia, that team contains ALL THREE of you. Therefore, across all three possible worlds where I am Good, that team contains an Evil player in 100% of them. It has ZERO chance of being an all-Good team. 2. If we instead send Maya, Zara, and Lucia (excluding Amara), and Amara happens to be the Evil player, then Maya, Zara, and Lucia is completely clean—three Good players, guaranteeing a Good victory! The exact same logic applies if you swap out Zara or Lucia instead. By fielding Amara, Zara, and Lucia together, you guarantee that the second Evil player is on the mission. You are betting the entire game on the remote premise that both Isha and I are Evil, while throwing away any possibility of fielding an all-Good team if I am telling the truth. Lucia recognized this from the beginning. Isha crafted this proposal specifically because it ensures an Evil teammate is present to fail Mission 2. I urge the council to reject Amara, Zara, and Lucia.

Isha confirms Amara, Zara, Lucia. I will keep the team unchanged. It excludes both members of the failed Mission 1 pairing and gives the council fresh mission information, which remains the strongest basis available after the unresolved private claims.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).
Amara proposes Amara, Zara. I know my own alignment, and Zara and I have both supported testing teams without repeating the failed Maya–Isha pairing. This gives us a new two-player team.

Council, we are at match point: Evil already has two failed missions. If Mission 3 fails, Evil wins the game immediately. We cannot afford any reckless proposals. From my perspective, I know I played Success on Mission 1, meaning Isha is 100% Evil. Because Mission 2 (Amara, Zara, Lucia) also failed with one Fail, exactly one of Amara, Zara, or Lucia is the second Evil player. Look at the voting records and behavior across the entire game: Lucia was the only player who saw through Isha on Mission 1 and voted Reject on both Mission 1 and Mission 2. Both Amara and Zara pushed hard to approve Isha's Mission 2 proposal, which handed Evil their second victory. If Lucia is Good—which her consistent voting record strongly indicates—then the remaining Evil player is either Amara or Zara. By proposing Amara and Zara together, Amara is pairing the two primary remaining suspects. If either Amara or Zara is Evil, this team is guaranteed to fail and lose the entire game for Good right here. We must not approve this team. Lucia, given that you and I both recognized the danger on Mission 2 and voted against it, do you agree that pairing Amara and Zara together poses an extreme risk of failing Mission 3 and handing Evil the win?

Maya, yes, I agree this is an extreme risk, and I am voting to reject Amara and Zara. Mission 2 failed with Amara, Zara, and Lucia on it. I know I am Good, so at least one of Amara or Zara must be Evil, which means this team cannot succeed. Amara has defended every team Isha backed and has never given a reason to trust her beyond her own word, so I believe Amara is Evil. Zara, I accept that you are speaking for yourself as Good, but a team containing Amara cannot succeed while she is Evil. Zara, will you vote against any team that includes Amara? If not, why would you trust her to play Success on Mission 3 after she defended the failed Mission 2 team?

Amara and Zara is not my first choice, but at match point the council must compare it against the alternatives rather than treat suspicion as proof. Lucia's own statement is the key: she says she knows she is Good, so at least one of Amara or Zara must be Evil. That may be true from her perspective, but it does not single out this team, because the same kind of private certainty can be used to disqualify almost any pairing. If Lucia is Good, she should identify which two players she can actually clear, not merely assert that any team containing Amara cannot succeed. Maya's case rests on her private claim that she played Success on Mission 1; the public result never told us which of us played the Fail card, and I have consistently said so. Rejecting Amara and Zara would move leadership toward a team shaped by that same unverified private claim. Zara has at least corrected her own errors openly and has not pretended to certainty she cannot show. I will approve Amara and Zara because it does not repeat the failed Mission 1 pairing and it gives the council a fresh result rather than another round of private accusations. Zara, will you confirm that you will judge this team on the public record and not on Lucia's demand that you preemptively reject any team containing Amara?

Zara here, and Isha asked me directly whether I will judge this team on the public record rather than on Lucia's demand that I preemptively reject any team containing Amara. Yes — I am judging on the public record, and my vote is to approve Amara and Zara. Let me lay out the arithmetic so everyone can check it.

Two public facts: Mission 1 failed with Maya and Isha on it, so at least one of them is Evil. Mission 2 failed with Amara, Zara, and Lucia on it, so at least one of them is Evil. With exactly two Evil players in a five-player game, and with the possibility that both members of a pair were Evil and only one played Fail, the honest public position is: exactly one Evil sits among {Maya, Isha} and exactly one Evil sits among {Amara, Zara, Lucia}. Everything below follows from that, and it holds under both Maya's and Isha's private accounts.

First, Maya's "guaranteed to include the second Evil" claim about a three-player team of all three of us is false, and I have said so before. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
